## Project Details

```

CHALLENGE FIT

CARL by team Pale Blue Dot is a visual health monitoring tool that lets astronauts assess their own health during long-duration space missions and act on it. CARL gathers health indicators, evaluates them against NASA standards, explains every result in plain language and gives guidance on treatments, countermeasures and health improvements. It answers each question in the challenge: which measurements can be performed in space, why an exam is needed, how spaceflight hazards affect each indicator, when a result warrants attention, and what action prevents a critical health condition.

WHAT IT DOES

- Clickable 3D human figure: every body region is interactive; selecting it peels body layers and shows the function, readings, trend, NASA limit and health status of that system.

- Four body systems, five hazards: immune, skeletal, cardiovascular and behavioral health, plus space radiation and the closed cabin environment, mapped to the NASA Human Research Program five hazards of human spaceflight (space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, hostile closed environments).

- Health indicators: complete blood count (lymphocytes, white blood cells, neutrophils, monocytes, platelets, hemoglobin), bone mineral density (hip, spine, femoral neck), muscle strength, aerobic capacity (VO2max), ECG-monitored fitness test, 7-day sleep hours, reaction time and lapses (PVT-B, basis of the ISS Reaction Self-Test), career effective radiation dose, organ doses (blood-forming organs, circulatory system, central nervous system), galactic cosmic ray dose rate, solar particle event dose, cabin CO2.

- Color coding at a glance: four status levels (nominal, advisory, caution, warning), each with a color, an icon and a word, and a 0-100 score per body system.

- AI medical assistant: CARL monitors every crew member continuously, raises alerts unprompted, explains each deviation with its NASA source, answers questions, and acts through visible tool calls (request a test, highlight a body region, run a scan, look up a NASA limit, run a forecast, prescribe a countermeasure). The astronaut accepts or declines every proposal: human-in-the-loop decision support.

- Guided self-exams with simple instructions: blood panel (hand the sample to the centrifuge), bone density scan (pull the scan band over the hip), ECG fitness test (place three leads on the chest), reaction test (measures the user's real response times). No medical training is assumed.

- Measurement prompts: when a reading is out of date, CARL asks the astronaut to repeat the test as part of the mission routine.

- Dynamic charts: trend lines for every indicator and a draggable forecast timeline that projects each system to any mission day, with and without the accepted countermeasures, shown as two ghost figures.

- Countermeasures and treatment guidance: aerobic exercise, resistive exercise, bisphosphonate, immune support, sleep schedule, storm shelter, each with its NASA evidence source and projected effect.

- Gamification: weekly session ticks and a daily check-in for each countermeasure, gesture-based tests and a reaction game keep the crew engaged with health tasks.

- Live space weather: NASA DONKI solar flare and solar energetic particle events raise radiation dose and trigger shelter alerts in real time.

- Multiple environments: crew aboard a Mars transit vehicle, on EVA in a suit, and on Earth (post-flight reconditioning, backup crew training).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Deep space crews cannot wait for a flight surgeon: communication delay to Mars reaches minutes. CARL gives the crew Earth-independent medical autonomy: early detection before symptoms, explainable alerts, evidence-based countermeasures and a forecast of consequences. It reduces cognitive load, supports preventive medicine against bone loss, immune dysregulation, cardiovascular deconditioning, sleep loss and radiation exposure, and applies to Artemis lunar missions, Mars missions, space stations and analog or remote medicine on Earth.

HOW IT WORKS

A deterministic rules engine evaluates every reading against exactly one NASA limit or reference range and carries the provenance (document, revision, clause or dataset ID, link). CARL never invents a number: the language model refers to readings, limits and sources by ID and the panel fills them in from the rules engine, so every figure on screen is traceable to NASA data and hallucinated values are impossible by design. If the model is slow or unavailable, rule-based wording takes its place, so CARL keeps working without the model.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, SOFTWARE

TypeScript, React 19, Next.js 16, Tailwind CSS 4, Motion, Zustand; Unity 6 (URP, WebGL/WebAssembly) and C# for the 3D body view; Blender and Python for 3D models; Google Gemini API with function calling and streaming; NASA DONKI API; Vercel serverless routes with signed tokens, origin checks and rate limiting; Web Audio synthesized sound; Vitest unit tests, Playwright end-to-end tests, axe-core accessibility tests; typed JSON bridge shared by the web app and Unity. The Unity build is 13 MB compressed and runs at 60+ fps in the browser.

CREATIVITY

The body is the interface. The crew stand on a rotating 3D ring; the selected figure flies forward into a personal cabin; readings float beside the body, tied by leader lines to where they are measured; tests start with a physical gesture on a prop; CARL's actions are drawn on screen as a line from its mark to the target; a time slider shows the body's future.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Scientific validity (only indicators with a NASA limit or reference range are shown; every value cites its source), explainable and trustworthy AI, crew autonomy and astronaut authority over decisions, usability under stress (one glance shows what needs attention), accessibility (full keyboard control, screen reader support, WCAG AA contrast, status never by color alone, reduced motion), resilience (a flat 2D body view replaces the 3D view where it cannot load), performance and security.

USE OF SI

Super Intelligence tools were used: SI coding assistants (Anthropic Claude) helped write code, tests and documentation under team direction and review; CARL's language runs on a large language model (Google Gemini). No NASA branding is used or modified.

```
